speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (for the Minister for National Development) (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, there are practical difficulties to provide more heavy vehicle parking lots in residential estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (for the Minister for National Development) (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, these estates are highly built up; second, land is needed for housing and other community uses residents need; and third, we also receive feedback of residents' concerns on noise and above all, safety arising from heavy vehicular traffic in or near residential areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (for the Minister for National Development) (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ultimately, it is the responsibility of business owners to have parking solutions for the vehicles they own and also to work out with their drivers appropriate transport options to commute to work, especially for those who have to drive during the wee hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are quite a few occasions where I have come across drivers who actually have to sleep in the vehicles because they really cannot find a heavy vehicle parking lot and they have to park by the roadside somewhere and they are worried about summonses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I was wondering whether the Ministry can do some kind of review.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Technically, every single heavy vehicle that runs on the road in Singapore already has a designated lot and a VPC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The drivers that the Member referred to, there are already designated lots for their vehicles, by way of the VPC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I said earlier that numerically, there are more lots than there are vehicles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The problem that the Member articulated in context is largely one of localised mismatch of supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are a variety of instances, but let me draw to the House's attention, three situations that we can encounter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first situation is business owners want to park their vehicles after the working shift, near to their business premises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a factor of production; they went to keep it nearby for servicing, maintenance, security and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But they cannot find lots, because the parking in that area is heavily subscribed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The second situation is a bit more interesting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Business owners have a VPC for their vehicle, that means they have a certificate and a lot, but they are not permitted to park in the lot for which they bought the VPC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sometimes, we find that it is because the private operators of that particular parking lot is misusing the space, for example, using it to store goods, equipment for his own vehicles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a VPC on paper; the business owner buys it, can renew road tax and all, but for all purposes and intents, the business owner does not have a lot and the driver bears the brunt of it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The third situation is probably the one that Members see the most.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The vehicle owner has secured the VPC but the driver prefers instead to park as close to home as possible, often, in and around HDB residential estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But there are not enough of such lots and there is a waiting queue.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I said earlier in my reply that these lots are scarce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is demand for land and there is a lot of security and safety concerns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In these situations, the drivers have difficulty getting to and from the lot in which the owner has gotten.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The owner just gets a lot but leaves it to the driver to sort out his own commute.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If it is ending work at 11.00 pm, midnight or starting work at 2.00 am to 3.00 am, for some drivers, that can be a challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is largely because the company, the employer does not provide for that commute.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will look to address the three big scenarios in a number of ways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the first situation, we plan to inject more heavy parking lots in industrial estates where business owners have a lot of demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, URA and JTC will continue to mandate the building of heavy vehicle parks in heavy industrial developments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For new industrial estates and whenever older industrial estates are being re-developed, both HDB and JTC will inject more heavy vehicle parking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will be particularly useful for HDB industrial estates being redeveloped because they are not that far from some of our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the second situation, the phantom lots, it is an issue of enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The drivers who are faced with this ought to make a report so that the proper action can be taken.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the third situation, and this is the one we are most sympathetic about, when employers get a lot and it is far from the driver's home and the company does not provide or does not wish to provide a service to bring the driver to work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are looking at how best, through a number of levers, to get companies and businesses to meet the transport and commuting needs of their drivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are a number of areas that we need to look at and it is not an issue that is one dimensional.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I raised this during the Committee of Supply (COS) last year, which is about using other car park places available at night.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If you go to a sports stadium, the car parks at night are totally empty because there is nobody in the stadium.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can we not think about converting such places to become parking lots for heavy vehicles on a temporary basis?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Essentially, we are talking about more efficient use of land.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Whenever we talk about heavy vehicle car park lots, most of the time in the day, they are empty.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, we are keeping them empty in the day, only to be used at night.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can we not think of a way where we have lots of car park spaces that are for commercial or sports use and they are available at night, and we allow the heavy vehicle drivers to park there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A whole variety of out-of-the-box solutions is certainly being looked at all the time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The idea about parking space at stadiums, at schools for school buses, all these are things we look at.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to be mindful, of course, about the concerns that are raised about safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the car park is near or within residential estates, then, that poses concerns that residents will raise.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: What about working with industry associations or unions?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Individual companies arranging transport for one person may be difficult, but as an association or union, perhaps, they can cobble up enough companies and drivers to run a transport service circuit to address this location mismatch.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, 92% owned by businesses large and small and even medium size.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, there is a situation where the company buys the VPC for a location in Changi but the driver stays in Jurong.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another company may have bought the VPC in Jurong but the driver stays in Changi.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can we not have a matching system where they can just swop the VPC?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because currently, on its own, the company would not have the resources and the network to realise that there is an opposite match.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is about coordination at the broader level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From the company's point of view, if they know the driver lives in Jurong, they should try to look for a heavy vehicle park that is not that far away.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Businesses can play a part and they can have a conversation with their drivers to get a better sense of what their needs are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are many levels where people can play a part.
